title: Opening a Research Notes Section
text:
I am opening this section as a place for informal but careful writing about aerodynamics. The aim is not to replace peer-reviewed publications, but to create a space for reading notes, comments on scientific papers, experimental observations, and thoughts that may later grow into more structured work.
When I write about papers by other researchers, I want to focus on what I find physically interesting: the research question, the experimental or numerical strategy, the flow mechanisms involved, and the parts that connect with bluff-body and heavy-vehicle aerodynamics.
For paper commentaries, I will usually try to follow a simple structure:

What problem is the study trying to address?
What is the main physical mechanism or methodological idea?
What did I find particularly useful, surprising, or debatable?
How does it relate to wake dynamics, drag reduction, flow control, or experimental aerodynamics?

Some posts will be short notes. Others may be longer reflections on methods such as wind-tunnel testing, PIV, track testing, pressure measurements, or the interpretation of drag-reduction strategies. The common thread will be curiosity about separated flows and the practical aerodynamics of ground vehicles.

title: Research
text:
My research focuses on the experimental aerodynamics of bluff bodies and heavy vehicles, with emphasis on wake dynamics, pressure drag, flow separation, and passive or active strategies for drag reduction.
The central objective is to connect the underlying flow physics of three-dimensional separated wakes with aerodynamic performance in configurations relevant to ground vehicles.

title: Research
text:
Research Themes


Bluff-Body Wakes
Near-wake topology, recirculation regions, pressure recovery, wake asymmetry, and reflectional-symmetry-breaking dynamics.


Heavy-Vehicle Aerodynamics
Flow mechanisms relevant to square-back and heavy-vehicle geometries, including crosswind effects and practical drag-reduction constraints.


Flow Control
Passive and active control strategies, including adaptive flaps, base blowing, rear cavities, and self-adaptive devices.

title: Research
text:
Methods


Wind-tunnel experiments: controlled measurements of forces, pressure distributions, wake development, and drag-reduction performance.
Particle image velocimetry: two-component and flow-field measurements for characterising separation, recirculation, wake structure, and turbulence.
Track testing: aerodynamic assessment under more representative road conditions.
Data analysis: linking local flow organisation with global quantities such as drag, base pressure, and aerodynamic loading.

title: About
text:
I am José Manuel Camacho Sánchez, PhD, an experimental aerodynamics researcher focused on bluff-body wakes, heavy-vehicle aerodynamics, and drag-reduction strategies.
My work connects controlled laboratory experiments with applied vehicle performance. I have worked with wind-tunnel testing, particle image velocimetry (PIV), pressure and force measurements, track testing, and the analysis of passive and active flow-control devices.
